title: The Handshake in Orbit
text:
In 1972, in a period of easing Cold War tensions, the United States and the Soviet Union agreed to fly a joint space mission. The two countries had spent fifteen years racing each other into space, and their spacecraft were not built to work together.

Engineers from both sides met repeatedly over three years to solve the practical problems. They designed a new docking system that either craft could use, and a docking module that served as an airlock between the American cabin, with its low-pressure pure oxygen atmosphere, and the Soviet one, which used air at normal pressure. The crews trained in each other's countries. The Americans, Thomas Stafford, Vance Brand and Deke Slayton, learned Russian; the cosmonauts, Alexei Leonov and Valery Kubasov, learned English. To make communication easier, each side spoke the other's language. Leonov joked that Stafford's accented Russian was a third language, "Oklahomski."

On 15 July 1975 Soyuz 19 and an Apollo spacecraft launched hours apart. On 17 July they docked in orbit. Stafford and Leonov opened the hatches and shook hands, a moment broadcast around the world. For about two days the crews visited each other's craft, shared meals, exchanged gifts and conducted joint experiments.

Political relations soured again later in the 1970s. But the mission laid foundations for later cooperation, including Shuttle flights to the Mir station and the International Space Station.
lesson: Rivals can work together when they share a goal larger than themselves. Meeting the other side halfway, even in language, builds trust.
people: Thomas Stafford, Vance Brand, Deke Slayton, Alexei Leonov, Valery Kubasov
source: NASA, Apollo-Soyuz Test Project records (NASA SP-4209, The Partnership, 1978)
